title: One plane, on time
hook: A new airline with no planes orders 100 of them. Then the whole industry starts losing money.

profit.label: Cash
profit.hint: Money in the bank to get through bad times

future.label: Edge
future.hint: How far ahead of rival airlines you are

intro.text: Delhi, 2005. A year ago India opened its skies to new airlines, and about six have started since. You and a co-founder, backed by the travel group InterGlobe, want to build a low-fare airline for ordinary Indians. Right now, you have no planes, no pilots and no flights.

s_goal.text: Three airlines, Jet, Kingfisher and Air India, carry nearly 8 in 10 Indian flyers. But the economy is booming, air travel could grow by up to a fifth every year, and Airbus thinks 100 million more Indians could start flying by 2010. To catch that wave you need planes, and a new plane takes more than a year to arrive.

d1.title: How big to start?
d1.setup: You are at the Paris Air Show, where airlines from around the world buy their planes. Kingfisher, the glamour airline, has just ordered giant superjumbo jets. You have money from your backers, but you have not flown a single passenger yet.
d1.question: How do you build your fleet?
d1.advisor: If we start small, the risk is lower. But if the flyers arrive fast, the big three could get to them first.

options.label: Lease 10 used planes and grow as the flyers come. If the boom fades, you lose little.
options.outcome: You are flying within months, and your costs stay low. But with only 10 planes you are a small player, and every new route has to wait for another plane.
options.why: Starting small felt safe, but a small airline pays the most for every plane, every part and every pilot, and can't grab the growth when it comes.
options.better: Order many new planes of one type, so you get a bulk discount and simple, cheap operations.
options.takeaway: In 2005 you started small and safe, and gave up the cost edge a big, simple fleet would bring.

options.label: Order 100 new Airbus A320s, all the same type, before your first flight, to get a bulk price.
options.outcome: On 16 June 2005 you order 100 Airbus A320 planes, worth $6 billion at list prices, before you have flown a single flight. Your first plane arrives on 28 July 2006, and a week later you fly your first passengers, from Delhi to Imphal via Guwahati.
options.why: One big order of one plane type bought a bulk discount and made everything simpler: one kind of pilot, one set of spare parts, one way of working.
options.takeaway: In 2005 you bought big and kept it simple: one plane type, ordered in bulk.

options.label: Buy jets of different sizes, so every route gets a plane that fits it.
options.outcome: You can fly almost any route you want. But every plane type needs its own pilots, its own training and its own spare parts, so your costs rise before you sell a single ticket.
options.why: Each extra plane type adds training, spare parts and slow turnarounds. A low-fare airline can't carry those costs.
options.better: Pick one plane type and order it in bulk, so every pilot, engineer and part works on every plane.
options.takeaway: In 2005 you bought every kind of plane, and your costs grew with every type.

d2.title: What will you sell?

setup.text: It is 2006, and your new A320s are arriving. Air Deccan, India's first low-fare airline, sells very cheap tickets but is struggling, while Kingfisher sells glamour. And in India, a flight that leaves 15 to 20 minutes late is normal.

It is 2006, and your mixed fleet is arriving. Air Deccan, India's first low-fare airline, sells very cheap tickets but is struggling, while Kingfisher sells glamour. And in India, a flight that leaves 15 to 20 minutes late is normal.

It is 2006, and your leased planes are flying. Air Deccan, India's first low-fare airline, sells very cheap tickets but is struggling, while Kingfisher sells glamour. And in India, a flight that leaves 15 to 20 minutes late is normal.

d2.question: What kind of airline will you be?
d2.advisor: Late flights annoy people, but they still book. Free meals and low fares are what make them pick an airline.

options.label: Offer free meals and a business class, so flyers who pay more choose you over Kingfisher.
options.outcome: Flyers love the meals and the lounges. But every seat now costs much more to fly, and you are fighting Kingfisher for the same small group of people who can pay for comfort.
options.why: You copied the costly comforts of the airlines you wanted to beat, so you gave flyers no new reason to choose you, and your costs went up.
options.better: Keep fares low, cut the extras, and give flyers one thing they can count on, such as leaving on time.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you copied your rivals' costly comforts instead of giving flyers a new reason to choose you.

options.label: Sell the cheapest tickets in India, even below cost for now, to grab flyers before rivals do.
options.outcome: Your planes fill up fast, and the papers love your fares. But you lose money on every seat, so the more you fly, the more you lose.
options.why: Low fares only work when your costs are lower too. Selling below cost buys flyers with money you can't get back.
options.better: Keep fares low but above cost, cut the extras, and promise something your rivals can't, such as leaving on time.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you bought flyers with losses. Cheap only works when your costs are cheaper too.

options.label: Cut the free meals and the business class. Sell low fares, one class and a promise to leave on time.

outcome.text: You launch with one class only: no business seats, no free meals, no loyalty points, just snacks for sale. Your big promise is simple: your flight leaves on time. Because every plane is an A320, crews work faster, and a plane can be ready to fly again in 20 to 30 minutes.
You launch with one class and a promise to leave on time. Flyers like it, but your mixed fleet makes the promise hard to keep, because each plane type needs its own crew and its own parts.
You launch with one class and a promise to leave on time. Flyers like it, but with only a few planes, one breakdown leaves you with no spare, and the promise is hard to keep.

options.why: You cut the extras most flyers didn't need and kept the one thing they valued most: getting there on time, at a low fare.
options.takeaway: In 2006 you sold low fares and on-time flights, and cut everything else.

d3.title: Paying for the planes

setup.text: Your airline is growing fast: six planes flew by the end of 2006, and nine more join in 2007. But your order is worth $6 billion at list prices, and a young airline can't pay that from its own pocket.
Your mixed fleet keeps growing, and so do the bills. You need many more planes, and a young airline can't pay for them from its own pocket.
Business is growing, and you need more planes, fast. A young airline can't pay for them from its own pocket.

d3.question: How do you pay for your planes?
d3.advisor: Banks will lend to us while times are good, and a plane we own is ours for good. But so is its loan, for many years.

options.label: Sell each new plane to a leasing firm, rent it back, and return it after six years.

outcome.text: You buy in bulk at a discount, sell each plane to a leasing firm around the time it arrives, and lease it back. Within about six years you hand it back for a new one. Big loans stay off your books, cash comes in up front, and your young planes are rarely delayed by repairs.
You sell new planes to leasing firms and rent them back. Without a big bulk order the deal pays you less, but big loans stay off your books, and your planes stay young.

options.why: You turned your big order into cash and kept your fleet young, without carrying heavy loans into the bad years.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you rented your planes instead of owning them, and kept your fleet young and your cash free.

options.label: Borrow from banks and own every plane. Over the years, owning costs less than renting.
options.outcome: The planes are yours, and so are the loans. Every month a big share of your cash goes to the banks, and you have little left over for a bad year.
options.why: Owning planes tied up your cash and loaded you with debt, just when a young airline needs room to breathe.
options.better: Sell new planes to leasing firms and rent them back, so the cash comes in up front and the fleet stays young.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you took on big loans to own planes you only needed to fly.

options.label: Rent older planes. They cost far less, and the savings keep your fares low.
options.outcome: Your bills drop, but old planes break down more often. Delays creep in, flyers notice, and your planes spend more days on the ground.
options.why: Old planes are cheap to rent but costly to keep flying, and every delay hurts an airline that wants flyers to trust it.
options.better: Keep a young fleet by selling new planes to leasing firms and renting them back.
options.takeaway: In 2007 you chose cheap, old planes, and paid for it in repairs and delays.

text.text: It is 2008, and the boom is over. Fuel prices have shot up, and fares with them. Last year Kingfisher's owner bought a big share of Air Deccan, and now Jet and Kingfisher are working together to cut costs. This year Indian airlines will lose $2.5 billion, about a quarter of all airline losses in the world. Your bank payments are due every month, whether your planes are full or not.

It is 2008, and the boom is over. Fuel prices have shot up, and fares with them. Last year Kingfisher's owner bought a big share of Air Deccan, and now Jet and Kingfisher are working together to cut costs. This year Indian airlines will lose $2.5 billion, about a quarter of all airline losses in the world. Your old planes make it worse, because they burn more fuel.

It is 2008, and the boom is over. Fuel prices have shot up, and fares with them. Last year Kingfisher's owner bought a big share of Air Deccan, and now Jet and Kingfisher are working together to cut costs. This year Indian airlines will lose $2.5 billion, about a quarter of all airline losses in the world.

d4.title: A storm for everyone

setup.text: Your free meals and lounges cost more every month. Some airlines are selling seats far below cost just to fill them, and rivals are joining hands to survive.
Your below-cost fares are now draining your cash fast. Some rivals sell even cheaper, and others are joining hands to survive.
Some airlines are selling seats far below cost just to fill them, and rivals are joining hands to survive. A few are in deep trouble.

d4.question: How do you get through the storm?
d4.advisor: Everyone says this is the time for a big move. A rival is cheap, and fuel is dear. Which risk do we take?

options.label: Buy a struggling rival while it is cheap, and come out of the storm twice your size.
options.outcome: You buy it cheap, but you also get its debts, its mixed planes and its unhappy staff. Fixing it eats up your cash and your time for years.
options.why: In a storm, buying a weak rival means buying its problems. It also broke your simple model of one plane type and low costs.
options.better: Stay on your own, keep costs tight, and keep growing while rivals struggle.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you bought a rival's problems and diluted your own strength.

options.label: Stay on your own and change nothing: same plane, same tight costs, same steady growth.

outcome.text: You keep flying only A320s, with one class and tight costs, and your 25th plane arrives in 2009. In the year to March 2009 you make a profit, while Kingfisher, Jet Airways and SpiceJet all lose money.
You keep costs tight and keep growing. It hurts, but when the storm passes you are bigger than before, and some rivals are much weaker.

options.why: While rivals lost their way, you kept doing the simple thing well, and you grew when others could not.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you stuck to your simple, low-cost model while rivals lost their way.

options.label: Park half your planes until fuel prices fall. Every empty flight you cancel saves cash.
options.outcome: You save some cash, but parked planes still cost money. When flyers come back, many of them are flying with your rivals.
options.why: Hiding from the storm saved a little cash but gave your routes and your flyers to rivals.
options.better: Keep your costs low enough to keep flying, and grow while others pull back.
options.takeaway: In 2008 you hid from the storm and gave rivals your routes.

text.text: By the end of 2010 you are India's third-biggest airline, ahead of Air India, the government's own airline. And Airbus has just launched a new version of your plane, the A320neo.
It is the end of 2010. You are still untangling the airline you bought and paying off its debts. Air travel is growing again, but your rivals are better placed to catch it.
It is the end of 2010. Your parked planes are flying again, but rivals took many of your flyers while you waited, and you are working hard to win them back.
It is the end of 2010. You have come through the storm, and Indians are flying again. Airbus has just launched a new, less thirsty version of the A320, called the A320neo.

d5.title: The next big bet
d5.setup: Very few Indians fly, so there is still huge room to grow, but nobody knows how fast it will come. Newer planes burn less fuel, but they cost a lot. And for the first time, you could also start flying abroad.
d5.question: What is your next big move?
d5.advisor: Our simple plan got us here. Do we keep building on it, change direction, or slow down?

options.label: Pause new orders and save cash. The last boom ended in a crash, and the next one could too.
options.outcome: Your cash pile grows. But rivals order new planes, and in a few years they have the newer, cheaper fleet, and the flyers that come with it.
options.why: India's flyers were still a small share of its people. Resting while the market grew handed that growth to rivals.
options.better: Order more of the plane that works for you, early, so you have the seats when the flyers come.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you rested while the market kept growing.

options.label: Buy long-range jets and fly to Europe and America, where each ticket earns far more.
options.outcome: The big jets are costly to buy and hard to fill, and your crews must learn a whole new kind of flying. Meanwhile, at home, rivals fill the gap you left.
options.why: Long-range jets broke your simple model of one plane type, short routes and quick turnarounds.
options.better: Grow with more of your own small planes, and fly abroad only to nearby cities they can reach.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you chased glamour routes and broke your own simple model.

options.label: Order 180 more small Airbus planes, most of them the new A320neo, for the flyers still to come.

outcome.text: On 12 January 2011 you agree to buy 180 more planes, 150 of them A320neo, worth $15.6 billion at list prices. Airbus calls it the largest single order for its passenger jets. On 1 September 2011 you fly abroad for the first time, from Delhi to Dubai, still on an A320.
You order many more of your small, less thirsty planes. It's a huge bet, but if India keeps flying more, you will have the seats.

options.why: You doubled down on what worked: one plane type, ordered big and early, ready for India's next wave of flyers.
options.takeaway: In 2011 you doubled down on what worked: one plane type, ordered big and early.

text.text: By October 2011 you are the only big Indian airline making a profit. A year later Kingfisher's planes stop flying and its licence is suspended, and you add flights to fill the gap. In 2012 you carry more passengers than any other airline in India.
Your simple, on-time airline pulls ahead while rivals with heavy costs struggle. Within a few years you are one of the biggest airlines in India.
Your airline survives the hard years, but the rival you bought keeps slowing you down. You are one of many airlines, never clearly ahead.
Your flyers like the comfort, but your costs stay high, and you never pull clearly ahead of the low-fare airlines.
Your airline survives the hard years, but it is one of many. With higher costs than it could have had, it never pulls clearly ahead of its rivals.

collapse.title: Grounded
collapse.text: High costs and debts catch up with you. Like several Indian airlines of this time, your planes go back to their owners and your flights stop.

fired.title: The board lets you go
fired.text: Three costly calls are too many. Your board loses faith in you and asks someone else to fly the airline through the hard years ahead.

realHistory: IndiGo ordered 100 Airbus A320s in June 2005, before it had flown at all, and flew its first flight in August 2006. It flew one plane type with one class, sold no free meals, promised on-time flights, and paid for planes by selling them to leasing companies and renting them back. In the year to March 2009, when most Indian airlines lost money, IndiGo made a profit. In 2011 it ordered 180 more A320-family planes and began flying abroad. In October 2012 Kingfisher stopped flying and its licence was suspended, and in 2012 IndiGo carried more passengers than any other Indian airline.
